2.text: The title shifts the focus from single-model refinement to population-level search over many candidate models.

4.text: Lab 23 improved outputs; this lab improves the configuration itself. The object being optimized changes from data to model population.

5.text: The key insight: instead of improving one model's outputs, we improve the model population itself through evolutionary pressure.

6.text: Each variant has different hyperparameters -- this diversity is what gives evolution something to select from.

7.text: Selection and mutation repeat over generations, so improvement comes from many small inherited changes rather than one optimizer run.

9.text: PBT is the core algorithm here: train many models in parallel, periodically replacing the worst with mutated copies of the best.

10.text: PBT is the direct template: train a population briefly, rank by fitness, then let strong members seed the next generation.

11.text: PBT combines hyperparameter search with ongoing training, so good settings can prove themselves under learning dynamics rather than static scoring.

12.text: Online selection is what distinguishes PBT from a static hyperparameter sweep: weak configs are replaced while training is still underway.

13.text: The population is not just ranked once. Replacement happens generation after generation, so search and learning are intertwined.

15.text: These related systems matter because they show the same outer-loop idea can optimize many kinds of candidates, not only neural net hyperparameters.

17.text: FunSearch is included as a conceptual cousin: both systems use an evolutionary outer loop to search over candidates scored by an objective.

23.text: The search space is intentionally small and interpretable, so each evolved improvement can be traced back to a concrete hyperparameter choice.

24.text: Validation loss is our fitness function -- evolution will minimize it by discovering good hyperparameter combinations.

25.text: That is the motivation for population search: a good region of configuration space can be found by repeated selection even when a single draw would likely miss it.

27.text: The docstring is explicit about scope: this lab teaches the exploit-explore control loop, not every engineering detail of production PBT.

612.text: If every survivor is the same size, say so in plain language. Top-k truncation with a low mutation rate collapses a gene pool this small very fast, and a real search needs a diversity floor: forbid duplicate genomes, keep random immigrants, or raise the mutation rate when variance drops. None of that is implemented here, and measuring it first is the point.

624.text: And if the population average got worse over the run, print that too. Children with fresh architectures restart untrained, so a population that keeps mutating keeps paying a restart cost, and "evolution improved the population" stops being a claim this run supports.

641.text: The numbered recap restates the algorithm as a control loop: initialize, train, evaluate, select, mutate, inherit, repeat.

652.text: Lab 23 improves training data (output quality); Lab 24 improves the model architecture and optimizer settings.

655.text: Lab 23 is like self-play refinement (STaR); Lab 24 is like natural selection -- fundamentally different strategies.

657.text: Exploit means reusing what already works; explore means mutating it enough to discover a better region of the search space.

658.text: Exploit: children inherit trained weights from successful parents, getting a head start on learning.

659.text: Explore: random hyperparameter mutations keep the population from settling into a local optimum.

662.text: PBT was originally designed to evolve learning rate schedules and data augmentation during training.

664.text: FunSearch uses the same pattern but evolves LLM-generated programs instead of numeric hyperparameters.

669.text: The compute point, restated with the run's own numbers: the matched-budget configuration advantage against the raw improvement figure. The gap between the two is what a compute ledger is for.

673.text: The lineage-age point. Equal new steps per generation is not equal total training, and the steps column is where that shows.

679.text: The diversity point, with the per-generation architecture curve inline. Once it reaches 1, selection has nothing left to select.

682.text: And the reason the reported winner comes from the archive rather than the final population: the two are frequently not the same model.

685.text: The closing claim is deliberately modest. Production PBT does discover schedules that would cost a researcher weeks, with populations large enough and mutation rates high enough that the gene pool survives, which is exactly the part a run at this size cannot show for free.
